text: She should have escalated it, and she did not.
They must have seen the email. It went to four people.
Somebody might have caught it, but nobody was looking.
He needn't have worried. The clause was never triggered.
She should have escalated it to one named person.
The firm should not have signed off on it without a second read.
She cannot have read it. It arrived after she left.
She needn't have worried about looking foolish.

People come to these panels expecting a moral question, and it is not one. There is a test, and the test is boring: what would a reasonable person in the same job, on the same afternoon, with the same workload, have done. If a reasonable person would have caught it, the word stops being oversight and starts being something else, and everybody in the room can feel the temperature change when that happens. Now, about the trainee. She did the hardest part, and I want that written down. Noticing is the hard part. Anybody can act on a problem once four partners agree it exists. What she should have done was escalate it, properly, to one person by name, and I will say in her defence that at twenty-four almost nobody does, because escalating feels like accusing four senior people of not reading their own email. The thing panels almost always get wrong is that they go looking for the person instead of the safeguard. We had a safeguard. A flagged inconsistency needs a second read before sign-off. It did not run. Nobody switched it off, so somebody, at some point, must have decided quietly that the second read was optional, and that decision is older than this file and bigger than anybody in this room.

It was one line, at the bottom of an email about three other things. And I want to be honest about why I wrote it that way, because for a long time I told myself it was because I was busy. It was not. I wrote it small on purpose. If I was wrong about the clauses, a small sentence at the bottom of a long email could be missed, and nobody would remember that I had made four senior people stop and check something for nothing. That was the fear. Not being wrong about the contract. I was fairly sure about the contract. The fear was being the person who wasted everybody's afternoon and then turned out to have misread it. Two years on, I know how ridiculous that sounds, and I also know that everybody I trained with did exactly the same thing. What do I do now? I say it twice. Once in writing, and once out loud to one person by name, and I finish with a sentence I stole from somebody more senior than me: tell me if this is nothing. It gives the other person somewhere easy to go, and it means the thing has been said in a room, out loud, where an email cannot be scrolled past.

She cannot have read it. It arrived after she left.
